# History of Johnson & Johnson: Timeline and Facts
## Johnson & Johnson Founding
Johnson & Johnson  (**JNJ**)  began as a small company that created surgical dressings.

In 1886, the pharmacist Robert Wood Johnson formed a new company with his brothers James Wood Johnson and Edward Mead Johnson.
The brothers founded their company based on Joseph Lister’s then-recent research into the nature of airborne germs and infectious disease. The new company would develop sterilization techniques and surgical dressings, hoping to create a more effective form of post-operative sterilization than Lister’s approach of spraying operating rooms with carbolic acid. The brothers formally incorporated their company in 1887 as Johnson & Johnson.

- 1886 – The Johnson brothers found their company based on the discoveries of Joseph Lister.
- 1887 – Johnson & Johnson is formally incorporated.
- 1888 – The company produces its first two products: a mainstream manual on treating injuries and the first mass-market first-aid kit.

These ridiculous age gaps don't register right away. This is partially because they're still fairly common in Hollywood, but also because while both Johnson and Statham have been making movies for around 20 years, neither of them feel like past-their-prime action heroes ready to sign up for  The Expendables .

It wants this so badly that the movie stops cold several times for superstar comic-relief cameos, advertising its own bigness, reminding the audience that Leitch last made the cartoony  Deadpool 2 . But these interludes aren't as fun (or as funny) as the movie's car-careening action sequences, or an early split-screen introduction that shows the heroes' contrasting morning routines. It's still fun to watch Johnson and Statham bicker. But the self-conscious japery brings them closer than expected to  Expendables territory, and allows Vanessa Kirby to run away with the movie. Before founding the company, Robert had visited the 1876 [world’s fair](https://britannica.com/topic/worlds-fair) in [Philadelphia](https://britannica.com/place/Philadelphia), where he attended a talk by Dr. [Joseph Lister](https://britannica.com/biography/Joseph-Lister-Baron-Lister-of-Lyme-Regis) on his new approach to surgery that involved [sterilization](https://britannica.com/science/sterilization-medicine) of tools and [antiseptic](https://britannica.com/science/antiseptic) dressings.

In 1932, Robert Wood Johnson II became the company’s chairman. A decade later, he was appointed by President [Franklin D. Roosevelt](https://britannica.com/biography/Franklin-D-Roosevelt) as head of the Smaller War Plants Corporation, where he oversaw wartime contracts for U.S. factories with fewer than 500 employees. ## Overview  
Johnson & Johnson (J&J) is a prominent American multinational corporation that develops, manufactures, and distributes medical devices, pharmaceuticals, and diagnostic equipment. Headquartered in New Brunswick, New Jersey, the publicly traded enterprise operates as one of the world’s largest healthcare corporations.
The enterprise was established in January 1886 in New Brunswick, New Jersey, by three brothers: Robert Wood Johnson, James Wood Johnson, and Edward Mead Johnson. Inspired by English surgeon Joseph Lister’s groundbreaking research into airborne antiseptic procedures, the founders set out to commercialize ready-to-use, sterile surgical dressings.
The corporation incorporated in 1887 and expanded rapidly throughout the early 20th century, introducing mass-market consumer safety lines, including commercial first-aid kits in 1888 and sanitary products in 1894. Under the executive leadership of Robert Wood Johnson II during the Great Depression, the company codified its decentralized operating model and drafted the formal “Johnson & Johnson Credo” in 1943.

Johnson & Johnson was founded in 1886 by [Robert Wood Johnson](https://britannica.com/money/Robert-Wood-Johnson), alongside his brothers, James Wood Johnson and Edward Mead Johnson. The first factory was located in [New Brunswick](https://britannica.com/place/New-Brunswick-New-Jersey), [New Jersey](https://britannica.com/place/New-Jersey). As a young man, Robert had apprenticed at his family’s pharmacy, Wood & Tittamer, in [Poughkeepsie](https://britannica.com/place/Poughkeepsie), [New York](https://britannica.com/place/New-York-state). There, he learned to create medicated plasters, a popular 19th century remedy consisting of adhesive patches that delivered medication through the skin. He then moved to [New York City](https://britannica.com/place/New-York-City), where he worked as a [pharmaceutical](https://britannica.com/technology/pharmaceutical) wholesaler.
Before founding the company, Robert had visited the 1876 [world’s fair](https://britannica.com/topic/worlds-fair) in [Philadelphia](https://britannica.com/place/Philadelphia), where he attended a talk by Dr. [Joseph Lister](https://britannica.com/biography/Joseph-Lister-Baron-Lister-of-Lyme-Regis) on his new approach to surgery that involved [sterilization](https://britannica.com/science/sterilization-medicine) of tools and [antiseptic](https://britannica.com/science/antiseptic) dressings.

In 1932, Robert Wood Johnson II became the company’s chairman. A decade later, he was appointed by President [Franklin D. Roosevelt](https://britannica.com/biography/Franklin-D-Roosevelt) as head of the Smaller War Plants Corporation, where he oversaw wartime contracts for U.S. factories with fewer than 500 employees. The company went public in 1944, with annual sales of about $95 million.
